mcqs.question: A company has an unpatched library with a known code-execution flaw, but no known attacker group is currently targeting it and no public exploit exists. Precisely, what does the company have?
options: A threat, since the flaw could theoretically be used against them
An exploit, since the flaw is documented
A vulnerability, with risk depending on the (currently low) likelihood a threat actor develops or uses an exploit against it
No security issue at all, since nothing is actively attacking it
mcqs.explanation: The flaw itself is a vulnerability — it exists independent of whether anyone is currently attacking it. Without a known threat actor or exploit in play, the associated risk (likelihood × impact) is currently low, but the vulnerability is real and worth tracking since either could appear later.

mcqs.question: Two vulnerabilities are the same underlying bug class, but one requires network access with no privileges and the other requires an attacker to already be logged in locally with elevated rights. Why do they get very different CVSS scores?
options: CVSS scores are randomly assigned by the reporting researcher
Only network-exploitable bugs are eligible for a CVSS score at all
CVSS ignores attack vector and privileges entirely, scoring only impact
CVSS explicitly factors in attack vector and privileges required, so a remotely exploitable, unprivileged bug scores far higher than the same bug class requiring existing elevated local access
mcqs.explanation: CVSS is built from metrics including attack vector and privileges required specifically so that two instances of the same bug class score differently based on how easy they are to reach and trigger — a remote, unprivileged path is far more dangerous in practice than one already requiring elevated local access.

mcqs.question: You see the CVSS vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/C:H/I:H/A:H on a new finding. Without looking up the numeric score, what does this vector already tell you?
options: It's a low-severity bug because it lacks a privilege escalation component
It's a worst-case profile — remotely exploitable, low complexity, no privileges or user interaction needed, and high impact across confidentiality, integrity, and availability
It only affects availability, not confidentiality or integrity
It requires physical access to exploit
mcqs.explanation: Each letter maps to a specific condition: AV:N is network-reachable, AC:L is no special conditions, PR:N and UI:N mean no privileges or clicks needed, and H/H/H is full impact on all three CIA properties — together, the profile of a critical, easily reached vulnerability, which is exactly what pushes a score toward the top of the scale.

mcqs.question: A CVSS 9.8 remote code execution exists in a library only called by an isolated internal batch job with no internet access and no untrusted input. A CVSS 5.3 bug lets any unauthenticated user leak another user's session token via a public endpoint. Which should a risk-aware team fix first?
options: The 5.3 bug — it's live and trivially exploitable by anyone right now, while the 9.8's actual reachability in this environment is effectively zero
The 9.8 bug, always, because CVSS score alone determines priority regardless of context
Neither — CVSS scores below 7 never need to be fixed
Both simultaneously, since CVSS scores must always be addressed within the same sprint
mcqs.explanation: CVSS scores severity in the abstract, not exploitability in your specific environment — the 9.8 bug's vulnerable path is unreachable here, while the lower-scored bug is actively exploitable by anyone. Prioritizing by raw score alone, without checking reachability, is exactly the mistake this comparison illustrates.

mcqs.question: In the Monday-morning triage example, why does the security team schedule the CVSS 9.8 library bug for a routine dependency bump instead of an emergency fix?
options: Because CVSS 9.8 findings are always false positives

Because the vulnerable code path is not reachable in this deployment — no internet access and no untrusted input reach it — so its actual exploitability here is near zero despite the high abstract score
Because emergency fixes are never justified for library dependencies
Because the finding was reported by an automated scanner rather than a human researcher
mcqs.explanation: The score reflects the vulnerability's severity in the abstract; the team's own risk-aware analysis of reachability in their specific deployment is what actually determines urgency. A CVE with no path to being triggered in your environment is a very different risk than the same CVE on an internet-facing, untrusted-input path.

mcqs.question: A team sets a fixed SLA to patch every vulnerability scoring 9.0+ within 48 hours, regardless of whether the vulnerable code path is ever reached in their deployment. What's the risk of this policy?
options: It has no downside, since patching quickly is always strictly better regardless of context
It will burn scarce engineering time on unreachable, non-exploitable findings while a lower-scored but genuinely live and reachable vulnerability waits in the backlog
CVSS scores above 9.0 are always false positives and shouldn't be patched at all
The SLA will cause every patch to introduce new vulnerabilities
mcqs.explanation: A fixed SLA keyed purely to the raw score, without an exposure or reachability check, misallocates the team's scarcest resource — engineering time — toward bugs that may never be exploitable in that environment, while a lower-scored but reachable bug sits unaddressed. This is the exact failure mode the CVSS-vs-exposure comparison earlier in the topic illustrates.
